/pages/about.html.about.title: About
/pages/about.html.about.p1: Product Leader at the crossroads of design and management, 12+ years of experience*. Currently Lead Product Designer & Product Manager at TNS (The Next Stories), maker of Autoya — B2B/B2C automotive SaaS.
/pages/about.html.about.p2: I drive the vision, the design system and end-to-end delivery with a team of 6 (back, front, mobile, design). Shipped on the App Store and Google Play in December 2025.
/pages/about.html.about.p3: I love going architecture-first: Cursor Rules, formalized PRDs, a clear Definition of Done. I'm also into purposeful motion (GSAP, physics-based easing) and weaving AI workflows into user research and delivery.
/pages/about.html.about.p4: Before TNS, I was the first design hire at Merim Groupe, an agency designer at The Design Crew (Pass Culture, Vendredi, Heetch), and freelanced on Eximion.
/pages/about.html.about.p5: On the community side, I volunteer with FrenchProduit (running meetups, speaker at FLUPA Nantes 2025).

_meta.title: Autoya — Mobile · TNS (The Next Stories) · 2025 — Jaime Villegas Maira
_meta.description: Case study: Autoya — iOS / Android mobile app for car-dealership salespeople. Lead Product Designer & Product Manager at TNS (The Next Stories) — Flutter, monochrome design system shared with the webapp, App Store & Google Play release December 2025.

/pages/work/autoya-mobile.html.am.lead: A pro photo studio in a salesperson's pocket.
/pages/work/autoya-mobile.html.am.desc1: B2B/B2C mobile app for car dealerships: capture, AI cut-out and vehicle listing publishing. Flutter, iOS + Android.
/pages/work/autoya-mobile.html.am.desc2: Lead Product Designer & Product Manager, paired with the CTO. Live on App Store and Google Play since December 2025.
/pages/work/autoya-mobile.html.am.thumb1: Immersive onboarding — first launch, preference calibration.
/pages/work/autoya-mobile.html.am.thumb2: Discover — personalized vehicle feed, quick filters.
/pages/work/autoya-mobile.html.am.thumb3: Vehicle page — gallery, specs, purposeful motion.
/pages/work/autoya-mobile.html.am.thumb4: Paywall & in-app purchase — credit packs, RevenueCat, IAP.
/pages/work/autoya-mobile.html.am.role.lead: End-to-end product ownership: vision, roadmap, prioritization, specs, design system, delivery.
/pages/work/autoya-mobile.html.am.role.p: I lead a team of 5 developers (backend, web front, Flutter, tech lead) and 1 product designer, working directly with the CEO and CTO. I own the trade-offs in front of clients (Ewigo, Dubreuil, CentraCar).
/pages/work/autoya-mobile.html.am.role.li1: Design — full design system (tokens, components, motion), 17-shots template, capture screens, paywall, onboarding.
/pages/work/autoya-mobile.html.am.role.li2: Product — quarterly roadmap, 20+ Linear cycles, 300+ issues, formalized Definition of Done, weekly sprint planning.
/pages/work/autoya-mobile.html.am.role.li3: Strategy — self-service monetization model (IAP + RevenueCat + Stripe), multi-org architecture, B2B/B2C pricing.
/pages/work/autoya-mobile.html.am.role.caveat: What I didn't do: the code (Flutter / NestJS), AWS infra, client contract negotiations (Sales / CEO).
/pages/work/autoya-mobile.html.am.dec.h2: The trade-offs that shaped the product
/pages/work/autoya-mobile.html.am.dec1.p1: First MVP: credits attached to the user. Problem spotted in discovery with the Dubreuil group — a salesperson who leaves takes their credits with them. I pushed a migration to an org-scoped DynamoDB ledger, FIFO, with a rolling 12-month expiry.
/pages/work/autoya-mobile.html.am.dec1.p2: Cost: 3 weeks of backend refactoring. Benefit: a viable model for multi-site groups — which make up 80% of target revenue.
/pages/work/autoya-mobile.html.am.dec2.h3: Defer haptic feedback, ship the in-app invite
/pages/work/autoya-mobile.html.am.dec2.p1: Two weeks from the Autoya Split, two candidate features were left in the sprint. Haptic feedback was more appealing in demos. The in-app invite closed the self-service onboarding loop — without it, no B2B virality.
/pages/work/autoya-mobile.html.am.dec2.p2: I called it for the invite and pushed haptic to the backlog. Unpopular with the team, but aligned with the strategy.
/pages/work/autoya-mobile.html.am.dec3.p1: Apple's «one active subscription per Apple ID» constraint blocked multi-account groups. Rather than wait for a perfect architecture (subscription groups + org switching), I scoped a Phase 1: consumable credit packs via IAP, subscriptions via Stripe web.
/pages/work/autoya-mobile.html.am.dec3.p2: Launch delay: −6 weeks. The model is imperfect, owned, and documented in the Phase 2 roadmap.
/pages/work/autoya-mobile.html.am.imp.li1: App published on the App Store + Google Play — December 2025.
/pages/work/autoya-mobile.html.am.imp.li2: 5 clients deployed in production: Ewigo, Dubreuil multi-site, CentraCar, Activ Auto, +1.
/pages/work/autoya-mobile.html.am.imp.li3: Point S field tests — SUS validated, salesperson insights integrated.
/pages/work/autoya-mobile.html.am.imp.li4: 20+ cycles shipped, 300+ issues closed, a team of 6 stable for 9 months.

_meta.title: Autoya — Webapp · TNS (The Next Stories) · 2025 — Jaime Villegas Maira
_meta.description: Case study: Autoya — B2B SaaS webapp for dealerships, networks and multi-site groups. AI cut-out studio, generation pipelines (composite, video, voice-over), native DMS integration. React 19, TypeScript, Feature-Sliced Design, monochrome design system.

/pages/work/autoya-webapp.html.aw.desc1: B2B SaaS platform for dealerships, networks and multi-site groups: AI cut-out studio, automated generation pipelines (composite, video, voice-over) and native DMS integration. A raw stock photo becomes a premium visual in a few clicks instead of a few days.
/pages/work/autoya-webapp.html.aw.desc2: Lead Product Designer & Product Manager — sole designer/Product Manager on the project, paired with the CTO. React 19 / TypeScript / Vite, Feature-Sliced Design architecture, monochrome design system shared with the Flutter mobile app.
/pages/work/autoya-webapp.html.aw.thumb1: Cutout Studio — magnetic canvas, AI cut-out, background templates.
/pages/work/autoya-webapp.html.aw.thumb2: Workflows — orchestrated AI pipelines (composite, video, voice-over, DMS).
/pages/work/autoya-webapp.html.aw.thumb3: Orgs & groups — multi-tenant, network view, shared credits.
/pages/work/autoya-webapp.html.aw.thumb4: Billing — org-level credits (FIFO + rolling expiry), Stripe self-service.
/pages/work/autoya-webapp.html.aw.role.lead: End-to-end product ownership of the web app: vision, roadmap, specs, design system, delivery — sole designer/Product Manager on the project.
/pages/work/autoya-webapp.html.aw.role.p: I work paired with the CTO, directly with the CEO. I own the automotive discovery, the SaaS solution framing, the B2B positioning and the credit-based monetization model.
/pages/work/autoya-webapp.html.aw.role.li1: Design — documented monochrome design system (CSS tokens, 30+ rules, shadcn/ui + Radix, Motion), detailed UX specs for dashboard, studio, settings, auth, onboarding.
/pages/work/autoya-webapp.html.aw.role.li2: Product — 15+ spec docs, end-to-end flows (auth → onboarding → production → DMS), backlog prioritization, acceptance criteria, 300+ issues across 20+ Linear cycles.
/pages/work/autoya-webapp.html.aw.role.li3: Strategy — multi-tenant orgs + groups model, credits + Stripe monetization, multi-site network targeting.
/pages/work/autoya-webapp.html.aw.role.caveat: What I didn't do: the code (React 19 / TypeScript / NestJS), AWS infra, the AI pipelines (CTO + backend team).
/pages/work/autoya-webapp.html.aw.dec.h2: The trade-offs that shaped the platform
/pages/work/autoya-webapp.html.aw.dec1.h3: Feature-Sliced Design as the architecture foundation
/pages/work/autoya-webapp.html.aw.dec1.p1: First framing: a classic layer-based front-end structure (components, pages, hooks). I pushed Feature-Sliced Design to isolate each business domain — auth, studio, workflows, billing, orgs — and keep velocity as the team grows.
/pages/work/autoya-webapp.html.aw.dec1.p2: Cost: an initial learning curve, 30+ architecture rules to document. Benefit: new features added without cross-cutting debt, no major refactor in 12 months.
/pages/work/autoya-webapp.html.aw.dec2.h3: A canvas-based Cutout Studio rather than a "fire and forget" upload
/pages/work/autoya-webapp.html.aw.dec2.p1: First MVP considered: a batch pipeline — upload, async AI processing, result delivered. Dealership discovery: salespeople want fine creative control (cropping, background, retouching) on every vehicle.
/pages/work/autoya-webapp.html.aw.dec2.p2: I scoped an interactive canvas studio with magnetic snap, background templates, one-click AI generation. Consumer-grade creative editing UX on a B2B tool — which became the differentiator against competing solutions.
/pages/work/autoya-webapp.html.aw.dec3.h3: Multi-tenant orgs + groups from the MVP
/pages/work/autoya-webapp.html.aw.dec3.p1: First scope: simple orgs, groups "later". But multi-site networks (Dubreuil-like) make up 80% of target revenue. Bolting it on afterwards = a painful migration for early adopters.
/pages/work/autoya-webapp.html.aw.dec3.p2: I pushed the orgs + groups structure into phase 1 — network view, shared credits, allocation per subsidiary. Cost: 3 extra weeks of design + backend. Benefit: immediate go-to-market on groups, no late migration.
/pages/work/autoya-webapp.html.aw.imp.li1: Web platform shipped 0 to 1 as the sole designer/Product Manager.
/pages/work/autoya-webapp.html.aw.imp.li2: Documented monochrome design system (30+ rules, CSS tokens, Radix + shadcn/ui components) shared with the Flutter mobile app.
/pages/work/autoya-webapp.html.aw.imp.li3: Feature-Sliced Design architecture — 0 major refactor in 12 months despite 15+ features added.
/pages/work/autoya-webapp.html.aw.imp.li4: WCAG AA, systematic Cypress + axe tests, native FR/EN i18n.

_meta.title: Merim — Design system · Merim Groupe · 2023–24 — Jaime Villegas Maira
_meta.description: Case study: Merim Groupe design system (food tech, restaurants). Tokens, components, documentation. The group's first design hire — building internal adoption, alongside the Checkout, Reporting and Drive-thru modules.

/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.lead: Getting a design system out of Figma — and getting the team to adopt it.
/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.desc1: Taking over a design system stalled for 6 months — a project inherited from an outside vendor, a pile-up of custom components, ageing interfaces. Foundations rebuilt on international standards, delivered in Figma and as a code library consumable by the whole front-end and product team.
/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.desc2: Lead Product Designer & Product Manager, first design hire. Governance through weekly contribution, progressive migration of Merim's app portfolio (Reporting, Checkout, Drive-thru).
/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.thumb1: Tokens & foundations — type, color, spacing, elevation.
/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.thumb2: Components — Figma library synced with the code library.
/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.thumb3: Reporting migration — pilot module, proof of value.
/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.thumb4: Governance — weekly forum, dev + product contribution.
/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.role.lead: First design hire at Merim. Taking over the design system project, rebuilding the foundations, setting up lasting governance.
/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.role.p: The DS had been going for 6 months under an outside vendor, with no real progress. Ageing interfaces, UX friction, a chronic mismatch between delivered mockups and the production render.
/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.role.li1: Design — tokens (type, color, spacing, elevation), Figma component library, usage guidelines, accessibility specs.
/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.role.li2: Product — DS roadmap framing, prioritization of the modules to migrate, acceptance criteria for each published component.
/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.role.li3: Governance — set up a weekly design system forum (front-end devs + Product Manager), an open contribution process, a decision log.
/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.role.caveat: What I didn't do: the component library code (front-end team), the budget arbitration with the outgoing vendor (management).
/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.dec.h2: The trade-offs that unblocked the project
/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.dec1.h3: International standards rather than a house identity
/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.dec1.p1: The inherited DS was built on a bespoke Merim identity, custom component after custom component. Every new need = a new one-off component, self-feeding debt — which is why the project had stalled.
/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.dec1.p2: I pivoted to foundations aligned with Material / HIG: patterns users already know, less technical debt, faster developer onboarding. Pushback: a dev team attached to the existing interfaces — "if it ain't broke, don't touch it." Brought on board through documented trade-offs and the weekly forum.
/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.dec2.h3: Governance through weekly contribution, not top-down
/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.dec2.p1: First design hire: the natural temptation is to scope everything solo and ship. But without adoption, a DS stays a Figma in a drawer — exactly what had happened to the vendor's project.
/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.dec2.p2: I set up a weekly design system forum: front-end devs + Product Manager around the table, component decisions made collectively, open contribution. Cost: co-built scoping is slower in the first months. Benefit: the DS became the team's shared language, not my personal project.
/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.dec3.h3: Progressive migration from Reporting, not big-bang
/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.dec3.p1: The vendor project aimed at a simultaneous overhaul of the whole platform — the reason for 6 months of no progress. I scoped a progressive migration, starting with the Reporting module: a manageable scope, limited operational criticality, an available team.
/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.dec3.p2: Benefit: proof of value delivered fast, trust earned, then rollout across the rest of the portfolio (Checkout, Drive-thru). Owned cost: two UXs coexist during the transition — a documented, accepted choice.
/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.imp.li1: Design system delivered in Figma and as a code library, consumable by the whole front-end and product team.
/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.imp.li2: Progressive migration of the app portfolio: Reporting → rest of the platform, with no product downtime.
/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.imp.li3: Mockup / production mismatch neutralized on migrated surfaces — end of design / dev back-and-forth on standard components.
/pages/work/merim-design-system.html.mds.imp.li4: A lasting weekly design governance forum, open contribution for devs and Product Managers — DS adopted as the shared language.

_meta.title: Merim — Checkout module · Merim Groupe · 2023–24 — Jaime Villegas Maira
_meta.description: Case study: Merim Checkout module — touch POS for quick-service restaurants. Optimizing critical workflows (order entry, modifiers, offline mode) and moving onto the Merim design system, without disrupting already-trained cashiers.

/pages/work/merim-caisse.html.mc.lead: A faster checkout, without relearning the moves.
/pages/work/merim-caisse.html.mc.desc1: Redesign of the Checkout module — touch POS for quick-service restaurants. Optimizing the critical workflows (order entry, modifiers, offline/degraded network mode) and moving onto the Merim design system, without breaking habits for already-trained cashiers.
/pages/work/merim-caisse.html.mc.desc2: Lead Product Designer & Product Manager, from discovery to delivering the JIRA specs for estimation sessions. UI run with a dedicated product designer.
/pages/work/merim-caisse.html.mc.thumb1: Main screen — product grid, persistent order, cashier shortcuts.
/pages/work/merim-caisse.html.mc.thumb2: Modifiers — persistent side-panel, order always visible.
/pages/work/merim-caisse.html.mc.thumb3: Offline mode — client-first operation, local queue, deferred sync.
/pages/work/merim-caisse.html.mc.role.lead: Leading the Checkout module redesign, from discovery to delivering the JIRA specs for estimation sessions.
/pages/work/merim-caisse.html.mc.role.p: UI run with a dedicated product designer. Critical workflows redefined with operators and cashiers in real conditions, moved onto the Merim design system as it was being built.
/pages/work/merim-caisse.html.mc.role.li1: Discovery — field observation, cashier and operator interviews, mapping the friction on the existing checkout.
/pages/work/merim-caisse.html.mc.role.li2: Design — flows, wireframes, high-fidelity screens on the Merim DS, touch prototypes, micro-interactions.
/pages/work/merim-caisse.html.mc.role.li3: Delivery — detailed JIRA specs per feature, acceptance criteria, estimation sessions with the devs.
/pages/work/merim-caisse.html.mc.role.caveat: What I didn't do: the code (Merim front-end team), the hardware strategy (terminals, screens, peripherals), change management at the operators.
/pages/work/merim-caisse.html.mc.dec.h2: The trade-offs that shaped the module
/pages/work/merim-caisse.html.mc.dec1.h3: Modifiers in a persistent side-panel, not a modal
/pages/work/merim-caisse.html.mc.dec1.p1: The inherited checkout opened a full-screen modal for every modifier (cooking, sauce, extra). Friction observed in the field: the cashier loses the order context, cognitive overload during a rush.
/pages/work/merim-caisse.html.mc.dec1.p2: I scoped a persistent side-panel — the order stays visible, modifiers are composed without breaking flow. Cost: less room for the product grid, a reworked hierarchy. Benefit: a continuous entry flow, fewer screens per order.
/pages/work/merim-caisse.html.mc.dec2.p1: A non-negotiable constraint: a cashier can't wait for the network to come back. First scope considered: partial blocking + a network indicator. I pushed client-first operation — the checkout takes payment even offline, local queue, back-end reconciliation when the network returns.
/pages/work/merim-caisse.html.mc.dec2.p2: Cost: back-end reconciliation complexity, conflict handling on payments. Benefit: guaranteed service continuity in restaurants, a strict operator requirement.
/pages/work/merim-caisse.html.mc.dec3.p1: Initial temptation: rethink everything from the new patterns. Reality: trained cashiers, memorized gestures, fleets in production. A radical redesign = heavy training and operational resistance.
/pages/work/merim-caisse.html.mc.dec3.p2: I scoped a redesign that preserves the known anchors (position of critical shortcuts, touch-zone geometry) and modernizes readability, hierarchy and density. Cost: strong design constraints, a few owned sub-optimal choices. Benefit: adoption without heavy training, minimized change management.
/pages/work/merim-caisse.html.mc.imp.li1: Checkout module redesigned, moved onto the Merim design system.
/pages/work/merim-caisse.html.mc.imp.li2: Modifier friction neutralized — a persistent side-panel replacing the full-screen modal.
/pages/work/merim-caisse.html.mc.imp.li3: Native offline mode: payment continuity during a network outage, deferred sync on return.
/pages/work/merim-caisse.html.mc.imp.li4: JIRA specs scoped, acceptance criteria documented, estimation sessions ready — discovery → delivery chain owned by design.

_meta.title: Merim — Reporting module · Merim Groupe · 2023–24 — Jaime Villegas Maira
_meta.description: Case study: Merim Reporting module (Dash) — real-time web platform for restaurant owners and managers. Sales, finance and customer-service KPIs, operational drill-down. Pilot module of the migration to the Merim design system.

/pages/work/merim-reporting.html.mr.lead: Read your restaurant at a glance.
/pages/work/merim-reporting.html.mr.desc1: Redesign of Dash — real-time web platform for restaurant owners and managers. Sales, finance and customer-service KPIs, operational drill-down. Pilot module of the migration to the Merim design system — first proof ground before the Checkout and Drive-thru modules.
/pages/work/merim-reporting.html.mr.desc2: Lead Product Designer & Product Manager, from discovery to delivering the JIRA specs. UI/UX run with two dedicated product designers.
/pages/work/merim-reporting.html.mr.thumb1: Overview — top sales, finance and customer-service KPIs.
/pages/work/merim-reporting.html.mr.thumb3: Drill-down — by product, time slot, employee, location.
/pages/work/merim-reporting.html.mr.thumb4: Pilot module — first proof ground for the Merim DS.
/pages/work/merim-reporting.html.mr.role.lead: Leading the Dash redesign, from discovery to delivering the JIRA specs for estimation sessions.
/pages/work/merim-reporting.html.mr.role.p: UI/UX run with two dedicated product designers. The module was chosen as the pilot for the migration to the Merim design system — proof of value for the DS on a manageable scope, before bringing in the critical modules (Checkout, Drive-thru).
/pages/work/merim-reporting.html.mr.role.li1: Discovery — interviews with restaurant owners and managers, mapping the recurring operational questions, framing the personas.
/pages/work/merim-reporting.html.mr.role.li2: Design — persona views, information hierarchy, visualization patterns, high-fidelity screens on the Merim DS as it was being built.
/pages/work/merim-reporting.html.mr.role.li3: Delivery — JIRA specs per feature, acceptance criteria, estimation sessions with the devs, go-live tracking.
/pages/work/merim-reporting.html.mr.role.caveat: What I didn't do: the code (Merim front-end team), the analytics data modeling (data team), the sales effort with the chains.
/pages/work/merim-reporting.html.mr.dec1.h3: Opinionated views per persona, not a dashboard builder
/pages/work/merim-reporting.html.mr.dec1.p1: Initial temptation: a custom builder à la Tableau / Looker. Reality: restaurant managers have no time to configure, and don't have the same questions. The owner watches revenue and margin. The manager watches the ticket and service. The accountant watches settlement and VAT.
/pages/work/merim-reporting.html.mr.dec1.p2: I scoped predefined views optimized per persona. Cost: less flexibility, some advanced analytics cases not covered. Benefit: immediate value with no configuration onboarding, readable in a few seconds.
/pages/work/merim-reporting.html.mr.dec2.h3: Progressive drill-down, no wall of numbers
/pages/work/merim-reporting.html.mr.dec2.p1: Stakeholders' first instinct: «show every possible metric on the home page». Risk: an illegible wall of numbers, info drowned out, a manager who works around the tool.
/pages/work/merim-reporting.html.mr.dec2.p2: I scoped a progressive hierarchy — top KPIs at the surface (revenue, average ticket, footfall), drill-down on demand into products, time slots, employees, locations. Cost: extra navigation for analysts. Benefit: immediate readability, no more «where's the info?» friction for the manager in a hurry.
/pages/work/merim-reporting.html.mr.dec3.h3: Pilot module for the Merim design system
/pages/work/merim-reporting.html.mr.dec3.p1: The DS project and the Reporting redesign were starting in parallel. Two options: wait for the DS to stabilize before redoing Dash, or use Dash as the first application ground — co-construction.
/pages/work/merim-reporting.html.mr.dec3.p2: I scoped Dash as the pilot module. Cost: an owned double effort — redo the module AND stress-test the DS on a real case. Benefit: tangible proof of value for the DS, a reproducible migration template for the critical modules that followed (Checkout, Drive-thru).
/pages/work/merim-reporting.html.mr.imp.li1: Dash redesigned, moved onto the Merim design system — first migrated module of the app portfolio.
/pages/work/merim-reporting.html.mr.imp.li2: Opinionated views per persona (owner, manager, accountant) — immediate value with no configuration.
/pages/work/merim-reporting.html.mr.imp.li3: Progressive drill-down from the main KPIs, no more wall of numbers.
/pages/work/merim-reporting.html.mr.imp.li4: Migration template validated on Dash, reused for Checkout and Drive-thru.
/pages/work/merim-reporting.html.mr.imp.li5: JIRA specs scoped, estimation sessions ready — discovery → delivery chain owned by design.

_meta.title: Merim — Drive-thru module · Merim Groupe · 2023–24 — Jaime Villegas Maira
_meta.description: Case study: Merim Drive-thru module — real-time monitoring system for fast-food managers. Per-lane operational steering, threshold alerts, intervention before friction. Continuous optimization of drive-thru efficiency and customer experience.

/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.lead: Spot drive-thru performance before it slips.
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.desc1: Redesign of the Drive-thru module — a real-time monitoring system for fast-food managers. Per-lane operational steering, threshold alerts, intervention before friction. Continuous optimization of drive-thru efficiency and customer experience.
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.desc2: Lead Product Designer & Product Manager, from discovery to delivering the JIRA specs. UI run with a dedicated product designer.
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.thumb1: Real-time steering — per-lane view, queue status, time in progress.
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.thumb2: Breakdown — order, payment, pickup time by step.
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.thumb3: Threshold alerts — color codes, manager escalation.
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.thumb4: History & benchmark — comparison by time slot, by location.
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.role.lead: Leading the Drive-thru module redesign, from discovery to delivering the JIRA specs for estimation sessions.
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.role.p: UI run with a dedicated product designer. Workflows redefined with QSR chain managers, operational constraints (readability at a distance, immediate action, a team in motion) framed in the field.
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.role.li1: Discovery — field observation during peak hours, manager interviews, mapping friction and the moments of intervention.
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.role.li2: Design — flows, real-time views, high-fidelity screens on the Merim DS, alert hierarchy, drill-down micro-interactions.
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.role.li3: Delivery — detailed JIRA specs per feature, acceptance criteria, estimation sessions with the devs.
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.role.caveat: What I didn't do: the code (Merim front-end team), the drive-thru sensors and instrumentation (hardware / back-end team), change management at the chains.
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.dec.h2: The trade-offs that shaped the module
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.dec1.h3: A per-step breakdown, not a global service time
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.dec1.p1: Simple first instinct: show «average service time» as the main KPI. But that number doesn't say where the friction is — a drive-thru slow on the order doesn't have the same fix as one slow at payment.
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.dec1.p2: I scoped a three-step breakdown (order, payment, pickup) per lane. Cost: finer instrumentation on the sensor and back-end side. Benefit: the bottleneck shows up immediately, the manager steps in where it's stuck.
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.dec2.h3: Real-time threshold alerts, not passive reporting
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.dec2.p1: Initial temptation: an analytics dashboard checked at the end of service. But a drive-thru's operational value is in immediate action — a customer who waits too long is a lost customer, and you can't win that back in a debrief.
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.dec2.p2: I scoped a real-time threshold alert system — color codes, visual signals, escalation to the manager on persistent overrun. Benefit: intervention before the queue forms, not after.
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.dec3.h3: A shared steering screen, not an individual app
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.dec3.p1: First scope: a manager app on a tablet, private supervision. Field discovery: drive-thru performance is a team sport — cashiers, prep, pickup — everyone needs to see the same indicator to align without talking.
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.dec3.p2: I scoped a shared steering screen, readable from a distance on a large kitchen display — XL type, strong contrast, status visible in 2 seconds. Cost: strong typographic constraints, limited info density. Benefit: performance becomes visible and collective, no more isolated «control tower» manager.
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.imp.li1: Drive-thru module redesigned, moved onto the Merim design system.
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.imp.li2: Service time broken down into steps (order, payment, pickup) per lane — friction localized at a glance.
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.imp.li3: Real-time threshold alert system — manager intervention before the queue forms.
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.imp.li4: Shared steering screen: performance visible to the whole team, operational alignment without talking.
/pages/work/merim-drive-thru.html.mdt.imp.li5: JIRA specs scoped, estimation sessions ready — discovery → delivery chain owned by design.

_meta.title: Eximion · Freelance · 2022–23 — Jaime Villegas Maira
_meta.description: Case study: Eximion — MVP of a crypto investment platform built to secure a fundraise. Product framing, founding design system (UI Kit), first brand identity. Freelance Product Designer.

/pages/work/eximion.html.ex.lead: Designing an MVP an investor can actually test.
/pages/work/eximion.html.ex.desc1: Freelance project for Eximion — MVP of a crypto investment platform built to secure a fundraise. A mixed audience: investors (proof of scalability and market potential), early adopters (usability validation), product team, stakeholders.
/pages/work/eximion.html.ex.desc2: Freelance Product Designer. Full scope: framing the MVP features, a founding design system (UI Kit), the first brand identity (logo, branding).
/pages/work/eximion.html.ex.thumb1: MVP dashboard — portfolio KPIs, recent transactions.
/pages/work/eximion.html.ex.thumb3: Platform UI Kit — type, colors, iconography, spacing, components.
/pages/work/eximion.html.ex.thumb4: Logo & branding — Eximion's first visual identity.
/pages/work/eximion.html.ex.role.lead: An end-to-end solo project — MVP product framing, founding design system, first brand identity.
/pages/work/eximion.html.ex.role.p: The challenge: take Eximion from pitch deck to a testable MVP, in a post-FTX crypto context where every detail counts to reassure an investor. Three interlocking deliverables: product, system, brand.
/pages/work/eximion.html.ex.role.li1: Product — framing the founding features: a Home Page with Dashboard (KPIs, recent transactions), Withdrawal, Deposit, User Settings.
/pages/work/eximion.html.ex.role.li2: Design system — Platform UI Kit Fundamentals: typography, palette, iconography, spacing, reusable components. A scalable base, delivered from V1.
/pages/work/eximion.html.ex.role.li3: Brand — Eximion's first logo, palette, visual tone, an expansion base for the post-raise product.
/pages/work/eximion.html.ex.role.caveat: What I didn't do: the code, the financial / trading strategy, the selection of listed crypto assets, the investor pitch itself.
/pages/work/eximion.html.ex.dec.h2: The trade-offs that shaped the MVP
/pages/work/eximion.html.ex.dec1.h3: A tight MVP scope on four core surfaces
/pages/work/eximion.html.ex.dec1.p1: The classic temptation for a fundraise MVP: pile up features to impress. But an investor tests depth, not surface — four screens that truly work beat twelve half-finished ones.
/pages/work/eximion.html.ex.dec1.p2: I scoped four critical surfaces: Dashboard (KPIs + recent transactions), Withdrawal, Deposit, User Settings. Owned trade-off: no advanced trading, no social, no alerts in V1. Benefit: an end-to-end demonstrable flow, a finished-product feel, immediate usability validation with early adopters.
/pages/work/eximion.html.ex.dec2.h3: Design system from the MVP, not after the raise
/pages/work/eximion.html.ex.dec2.p1: Temptation: ad-hoc design to move fast, «we'll redo it clean after the raise». Risk: immediate design debt, a painful post-raise overhaul — right when you need to accelerate to deliver on the promise made to investors.
/pages/work/eximion.html.ex.dec2.p2: I invested in the Platform UI Kit Fundamentals from V1: type, palette, iconography, spacing, reusable components. Cost: two to three weeks of upfront design. Benefit: visible consistency in the deck, product scalability, a clean foundation for growth — and a signal of product maturity to investors.
/pages/work/eximion.html.ex.dec3.h3: Brand identity alongside the product, not after
/pages/work/eximion.html.ex.dec3.p1: Possible choice: start from a placeholder name, design the identity after the raise. But to an investor, visual identity is a signal: brand ↔ product consistency = team maturity, the ability to execute over the long term.
/pages/work/eximion.html.ex.dec3.p2: I designed Eximion's first logo and brand identity (palette, tone, visual values) alongside the product screens. Benefit: perfect product ↔ brand consistency in the pitch deck, a solid base for post-raise expansion, a recognizable identity from day 1.
/pages/work/eximion.html.ex.imp.li1: MVP delivered on four core surfaces (Dashboard, Withdrawal, Deposit, Settings) — testable end to end by investors and early adopters.
/pages/work/eximion.html.ex.imp.li2: Platform UI Kit Fundamentals: type, palette, iconography, spacing, components — a scalable base ready for post-raise growth.
/pages/work/eximion.html.ex.imp.li3: Eximion's first identity: logo, palette, visual tone — brand ↔ product consistency ensured in the deck.
/pages/work/eximion.html.ex.imp.li4: Structured design ↔ development collaboration: a shared component system, deliverables ready for integration.

_meta.title: RestoApp · Freelance · 2025 — Jaime Villegas Maira
_meta.description: Case study: RestoApp — multi-tenant B2B SaaS platform for restaurant networks and venues. iOS app: per-venue real-time chat, sales analytics, network and subscription management, POS / delivery / booking integrations.

/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.lead: A platform that speaks restaurant, not generic SaaS.
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.desc1: Multi-tenant B2B SaaS platform for restaurant networks and venues. iOS app: per-venue real-time chat, sales analytics, network and subscription management, POS / delivery / booking integrations.
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.desc2: Freelance Lead Product Manager & Product Designer. Product vision, data architecture, Figma → SwiftUI design system.
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.thumb1: iOS app — operational home, KPIs, multi-venue selection.
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.thumb2: Chat hub — per-venue channels, DMs, operational hashtags.
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.thumb3: Web admin panel — network, accounts, integrations, subscriptions.
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.thumb4: Data architecture — shared TS contracts, Supabase RLS, authenticated WebSocket.
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.role.lead: A freelance project between Merim and Autoya — product and design lead on a multi-tenant SaaS platform for restaurants, from strategic framing to the coded design system.
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.role.p: A multi-channel platform: an operational iOS app (field teams), a web admin panel (management / franchise), a Node / TypeScript backend and PostgreSQL data via Supabase. Scope: strategy, segmentation, data architecture, design system, security.
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.role.li1: Strategy & segmentation — distinguishing operational users (team, managers) from buyers (Payer role), tiered plans (Starter / Premium / Franchise), B2B purchase journey.
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.role.li2: Mobile design system — brand colors, surfaces, a custom «Jaguar Exuberant» typeface, tokens (spacing, radii), a documented Figma → SwiftUI bridge, safe area and Dynamic Island handled.
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.role.li3: Product architecture — shared TypeScript contracts (models, API config, WebSocket events), business enums in French in the database schema, Row Level Security on the Supabase side.
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.role.li4: User flows — biometrics without sacrificing classic login, per-restaurant filter pills, sales drill-down, channels / DM separation (Slack-like usage), cross-filtering venue × operational hashtag.
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.role.caveat: What I didn't do: the entire codebase (mobile / web / back dev team), partner negotiations (POS, delivery, booking), the sales effort.
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.dec.h2: The trade-offs that shaped the platform
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.dec1.h3: Shared TypeScript contracts across iOS, web and API
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.dec1.p1: First reflex on a multi-channel project: let each team (iOS, web, back) define its own models and sync later. Reality: drift between channels is inevitable, and costs more to fix in production than to prevent.
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.dec1.p2: I pushed a `shared/` layer in TypeScript — models, API config, WebSocket events. A single source consumed by the web admin and the API, and aligned on the SwiftUI side. Cost: architecture discipline, a monorepo to maintain. Benefit: zero desync between channels, a model refactor propagated everywhere.
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.dec2.h3: Pricing plans written into the schema, not the marketing
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.dec2.p1: The classic temptation: define the plans (Starter / Premium / Franchise) as a «marketing» attribute and let the app handle the caps. Risk: Starter users bypassing limits via API, custom exceptions per chain, eroded monetization.
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.dec2.p2: I wrote the venue caps (1 / 3 / custom) into the shared models and into the PostgreSQL schema. Cost: tight plan / data coupling, a pricing change = a migration. Benefit: monetization by construction, no bypass possible on the code side.
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.dec3.h3: Strict French locale, no generic i18n
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.dec3.p1: The modern SaaS reflex: i18n from the start, English by default, French as a second language. Hidden cost: a product that speaks «translated English», with business vocabulary that rings false for French restaurateurs.
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.dec3.p2: I owned a strict France / Francophone positioning: business enums in French in the database schema, EUR formats and fr_FR locale, operational vocabulary native to the trade (channels, hashtags #shift / #affectation / #stock). Cost: an international pivot = a data overhaul. Benefit: a product that speaks right to its audience — no «translated from American».
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.imp.li1: Multi-channel platform delivered: SwiftUI iOS app + web admin panel + Node / TypeScript API + PostgreSQL via Supabase.
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.imp.li2: Shared models, config and events in TypeScript — zero desync between channels, refactors propagated by construction.
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.imp.li3: Pricing plans (Starter / Premium / Franchise) anchored in the schema — monetization with no bypass.
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.imp.li4: Per-venue real-time chat (authenticated WebSocket, per-venue broadcast, Supabase RLS) — trust and isolation by construction.
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.imp.li5: Mobile design system documented Figma → SwiftUI, custom «Jaguar Exuberant» typeface, safe area and Dynamic Island handled.
/pages/work/restoapp.html.ra.imp.li6: Native FR locale — business enums, EUR / fr_FR formats, operational vocabulary native to restaurants.

_meta.title: Vendredi · The Design Crew · 2023 — Jaime Villegas Maira
_meta.description: Case study: Vendredi — CSR employee-engagement SaaS platform. A four-phase project pivoting on the editorial concept «Temps Forts»: key moments of the year to spark collective momentum among employees. On assignment at The Design Crew.

/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.lead: Make CSR live month to month, not in a dropdown.
/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.desc1: The Design Crew assignment for Vendredi — a CSR employee-engagement SaaS platform. A four-phase project pivoting on the editorial concept «Temps Forts»: key moments of the year to spark collective momentum among employees.
/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.desc2: Product Designer on assignment. Leading the four phases — from framing the research to the A/B testing ahead of delivery.
/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.thumb2: Synthesis — participatory democracy, home redesign, search bar.
/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.thumb3: A/B testing — 5-user panel, relevance and comprehension.
/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.thumb4: Final delivery — Home, Voting System, Temps Forts page.
/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.role.lead: The Design Crew assignment, full project lead: Discovery, synthesis, design, A/B testing, delivery.
/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.role.p: Client brief: «How do we improve employee engagement by introducing Temps Forts?». Temps Forts are key moments of the year to spark collective momentum among employees around important themes (Pink October, the European Disability Employment Week, Sustainable Development Week…). The challenge: make the monthly mechanic speak to the employee without becoming yet another HR chore.
/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.role.li1: Discovery — user interviews on two axes: Awareness (what interests the employee in Temps Forts) and Empathy (barriers and motivations to commit to a cause).
/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.role.li2: Synthesis — three directions kept: participatory democracy, Home reorganization, and a search bar (bonus). Benchmark of related concepts: a video Hero section, spotlighting the Volunteers.
/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.role.li3: Design — final version on three surfaces: Home, Voting System, Temps Forts page.
/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.role.li4: Test & delivery — A/B testing on a real user panel before delivery, adjustments, final version delivered for integration.
/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.role.caveat: What I didn't do: the code, the CSR editorial strategy (Vendredi teams), the selection of partner associations.
/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.dec.h2: The trade-offs that structured the project
/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.dec1.h3: Empathy + awareness Discovery before any design
/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.dec1.p1: A framed client brief, a short sprint: the temptation to dive straight into design. I pushed for a real Discovery phase — two explicit goals (Awareness, Empathy), long user interviews.
/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.dec1.p2: Key learning: employees are strongly influenced by their social environment. They aren't looking for a cause to support — they want to be told about one. A typical quote collected: «I would be motivated to find someone to tell me about the association or a TV show, a documentary to inform me and see if there is a good atmosphere.» Pivot: from «how to search» toward «how to be reached».
/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.dec2.p1: Discovery delivers a lot of signals — the risk of running in every direction at once. I scoped three priority paths to answer «how do we use Temps Forts to reassure the employee and fit their everyday life?»:
/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.dec2.p2: Participatory democracy — make the employee an actor in choosing the themes (collective vote on the next month). Home reorganization — simplify, make browsing easier. Search bar (bonus) — smooth out the experience. Related benchmark: a video Hero section for immediate social proof, spotlighting the Volunteers community.
/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.dec3.h3: A/B testing before delivery — and what it revealed
/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.dec3.p1: The classic temptation on a short engagement: ship the final version without testing. I pushed for A/B testing on a real panel of service users: 5 people, 26–30 years old, 45–60 min interviews, on four goals (understanding the voting system, collective / individual relevance, interest in filters, smoothness of the Home).
/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.dec3.p2: Critical result: Votes 2 / 5 — «Did not make the connection between the voting system and the theme of the month.» An adjustment before delivery to make the vote ↔ theme-of-the-month link explicit in the UI. Benefit: a flaw caught BEFORE going to prod, not after.
/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.imp.li1: Final redesign delivered on three surfaces: Home, Voting System, Temps Forts page.
/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.imp.li2: Documented user Discovery — Awareness + Empathy, learnings usable beyond the initial client brief.
/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.imp.li3: Three research-anchored directions: participatory democracy, Home redesign, search bar.
/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.imp.li4: A/B testing done before delivery: a critical flaw identified (vote ↔ theme link) and fixed.
/pages/work/tdc-vendredi.html.ve.imp.li5: Monthly mechanic structured as an editorial narrative — collective vote, headline theme, multiple engagement entry points (challenges, missions, donations).

_meta.title: Heetch · The Design Crew · 2023 — Jaime Villegas Maira
_meta.description: Case study: Heetch — extending the ride-hailing app into micro-mobility (bikes, scooters). Client target: boost retention on short trips (< 3 km), +15% revenue, without disrupting existing driver activity. On assignment at The Design Crew.

/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.lead: Bring scooters into Heetch without rewriting habits.
/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.desc1: The Design Crew assignment for Heetch — extending the ride-hailing app into micro-mobility (bikes, scooters). Client target: boost retention on short trips (< 3 km), +15% revenue, without disrupting existing driver activity.
/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.desc2: Product Designer on assignment, in a TDC team. Leading the Ideation → Prototyping → Test journey, designing the onboarding, unlock, parking and outboarding screens.
/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.thumb1: Case study — micro-mobility extension, +15% revenue, trips < 3 km.
/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.thumb2: Ideation — benchmark, Success Keys, MoSCoW prioritization.
/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.thumb3: Prototyping — mid-fidelity flow then hi-fi v1.
/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.thumb4: Test — flow and affordance, quantified learnings (4/5).
/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.role.lead: The Design Crew assignment, in a team — a project structured in three phases: Ideation, Prototyping, Test.
/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.role.p: Client case: Heetch (a French Uber-like platform) wants to launch a micro-mobility service (bikes, scooters) to capture short trips. A triple constraint: +15% revenue, retention on trips < 3 km, without cannibalizing existing driver activity.
/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.role.li1: Ideation — benchmark of micro-mobility apps (onboardings, unlock, icons & affordance), formulating the Success Keys, MoSCoW prioritization.
/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.role.li2: Prototyping — a mid-fidelity user flow as the base, then hi-fi v1 on the key screens (map search, onboarding, parking, outboarding, rating).
/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.role.li3: Test — user panel, goals: understanding the flow and verifying the affordance of the new buttons.
/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.role.caveat: What I didn't do: the code, negotiating the bike / scooter operator contracts, the pricing strategy.
/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.dec.h2: The trade-offs that structured the project
/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.dec1.h3: Lean on the «collective unconscious» of existing apps
/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.dec1.p1: First reflex on a new service: invent Heetch's own patterns. Risk: forcing users to learn a system when they already know Lime, Tier, Bolt.
/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.dec1.p2: I scoped a structured benchmark on three axes — onboardings, unlock systems, icons & affordance. Key learning: there's a collective unconscious around micro-mobility, shared worldwide. Decision: lean on it rather than reinvent. Fast adoption, a minimal learning curve, design energy reserved for what differentiates Heetch (positioning, tone, values).
/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.dec2.p1: The classic temptation on a new service: pile up features to stand out. Risk: overloading a product users already have to learn.
/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.dec2.p2: I scoped a strict MoSCoW prioritization — Must Have: search map, unlock, parking, onboardings / outboarding. Should Have: eco values, young wording, rating. Could Have: route sharing, group ride. Won't Have: NFC unlocking. Plus two explicit Success Keys: simplify the onboardings, defer some features to iterations 2 / 3 to favor fast adaptation to the service.
/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.dec3.h3: User testing validates the initial Success Keys
/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.dec3.p1: The team got tempted into also covering the Could Have (Route Sharing, Group Ride) — a «robust» solution that goes beyond the MoSCoW. User test on a panel:
/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.dec3.p2: 4 / 5 — «Too much onboarding» (quote from Madjide D.: «To me it's advertising»). 4 / 5 — «Didn't understand some features» on Route Sharing and Group Ride (quote from Eloïse G.: «I don't know what this button does»). Learning: respect the user's time to mature with the service before innovating further — exactly what the initial Success Keys said. Corrective decision: back to the tight MoSCoW, defer the Could Have.
/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.imp.li1: Strategic framing of Heetch's micro-mobility extension — targeted KPIs (+15% revenue, retention on trips < 3 km), constraint respected (no driver cannibalization).
/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.imp.li2: Documented benchmark on three axes: onboardings, unlock, icons & affordance — a shared base of a grammar users already know.
/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.imp.li3: MoSCoW prioritization validated, two explicit Success Keys (simplify onboardings, defer non-MVP features).
/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.imp.li4: Mid-fi then hi-fi v1 prototypes on the full flow: map search, unlock, parking, outboarding, rating.
/pages/work/tdc-heetch.html.he.imp.li5: User test run: two quantified learnings (4 / 5), a corrective decision to return to the tight MoSCoW before production.

_meta.title: Pass Culture · The Design Crew · 2023 — Jaime Villegas Maira
_meta.description: Case study: Pass Culture (French Ministry of Culture). Discovery on 15–17 year-olds dropping off once the €20–30 grant is spent, then reframing the engagement strategy — the app shifts from cultural wallet to a social object among peers. On assignment at The Design Crew.

/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.lead: Keep 15–17 year-olds once the credit runs out.
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.desc1: The Design Crew assignment for Pass Culture (French Ministry of Culture). Discovery on 15–17 year-olds dropping off once the €20–30 grant is spent, then reframing the engagement strategy — the app shifts from cultural wallet to a social object among peers.
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.desc2: Product Designer on assignment. Guerrilla field study, user research, designing the solutions delivered as specs.
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.thumb1: Champs-Élysées guerrilla study — field insights into 15–17 cultural habits.
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.thumb2: Redesigned product page — real-time or classic, no video dependency.
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.thumb3: Social media integration — sync and native sharing.
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.thumb4: Sharing notifications — interactions among peers and siblings.
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.role.lead: The Design Crew assignment on the retention problem of 15–17 year-olds after the Pass Culture credit runs out.
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.role.p: Autonomous field Discovery, designing the solutions, delivery as specs. Client brief: the grant (€20–30) is spent fast, and the youth detach afterwards. The question: how do you maintain usage when the initial reason to use is gone?
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.role.li1: Research — a Champs-Élysées guerrilla study, 30+ flash interviews within the youths' daily routine, mapping their real cultural habits.
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.role.li2: Insights — 90% get their culture info via social media, 50% haven't used their credit yet, 100% know the app — the problem isn't awareness, it's the use value beyond the grant.
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.role.li3: Design — product page redesign (with or without video), rethought CTA, social media integration, a sharing-notification system between contacts.
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.role.caveat: What I didn't do: the code (Pass Culture teams), the cultural editorial strategy, the negotiation with social media partners.
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.dec.h2: The trade-offs that reframed the problem
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.dec1.h3: A guerrilla field study rather than pure analytics
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.dec1.p1: The analytics said «the youth detach once the credit is spent» — but not why. Temptation: push the data analysis further and infer.
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.dec1.p2: I scoped a guerrilla study on the Champs-Élysées — interception within the daily routine, flash interviews, usage observation. Cost: field time, a smaller sample than an analytics panel. Benefit: the youths' real sources of cultural info (social media), invisible in the app data.
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.dec2.h3: Graft the app onto social media, don't make it a hub
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.dec2.p1: Central insight: 90% of the youth get their culture info on social media. Business reflex: make Pass Culture the single destination (editorial feed, algo recommendations). But you'd be competing with Instagram and TikTok — a battle lost in advance.
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.dec2.p2: I scoped an integration strategy with social media rather than rivalry: sync, native outbound sharing, inbound notifications when a contact shares. Benefit: the app lives inside the existing social ecosystem, without asking the youth to change their habits.
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.dec3.h3: Post-credit pivot: from wallet to social object
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.dec3.p1: Pass Culture's business logic = a grant to consume. Once consumed, the app loses its reason to exist. First scope: extend usage through paid recommendations, partner loyalty cards.
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.dec3.p2: I pivoted to peer and sibling interactions as the retention engine — the app becomes a place for cultural sharing, independent of the credit. Notifications when a contact shares, exchanges, recommendations between young people. Benefit: the use value outlives the credit, aligned with the Pass Culture mission (democratize culture, not just subsidize it).
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.imp.li1: Documented field diagnosis: 90% / 50% / 100% — actionable insights beyond the app analytics.
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.imp.li2: Product page redesigned, real-time or classic, no video dependency — improved accessibility and conversion.
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.imp.li3: Main CTA optimized for visibility and conversion rate.
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.imp.li4: Social media integration strategy: sync, native sharing, notifications between contacts.
/pages/work/tdc-passculture.html.pc.imp.li5: Reframing of the business problem: post-credit, the app stops being a wallet and becomes a social object.

_meta.title: Tie Break · Side project · 2023 — Jaime Villegas Maira
_meta.description: Case study: Tie Break — iOS padel app. Side project, product design focused on the action during the match rather than a post-game recap.

/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.lead: The padel app that lives in the moment, not in your pocket.
/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.desc1: Side project — an iOS app for the French padel boom. The sport is exploding (995 courts in 2021, 1,339 in 2022, a target of 2,000 by 2024 driven by the FFT and the French National Sports Agency). Tie Break offers a directory of tennis / padel courts, a smartwatch-connected live score, a ranking among friends, and a brand identity built to stand out.
/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.desc2: Product Designer & Brand Designer. Full scope: product, visual identity, logo, high-fidelity UI.
/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.thumb1: Onboarding — logo, splash, native iOS login.
/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.thumb2: Friends Ranking — ranking among friends, W/L stats.
/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.thumb3: Roland-Garros court page — match in progress, live score.
/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.thumb4: Smartwatch sync — score on the wrist, game performance.
/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.role.lead: An end-to-end side project — from market framing to delivering the high-fidelity screens, including the full brand identity.
/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.role.p: Padel is exploding in France: the ecosystem is growing (clubs, courts, players), but the digital experience stays fragmented. Three personas addressed: club admins (court management), casual players (booking, community), enthusiasts (performance tracking, rankings).
/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.role.li1: Product — a directory of tennis / padel courts, a court page with match in progress, live score, ranking among friends, smartwatch integration.
/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.role.li2: UI — native iOS components (gestures, animations, system dark mode), immersive photography, tight typographic hierarchy.
/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.role.li3: Brand — logo, a clay-court + ball-yellow palette, a playful visual tone aligned with the sporting gesture.
/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.role.caveat: What I didn't do: the code (concept, not shipped to prod), negotiating club partnerships, the sports asset modeling.
/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.dec.h2: The trade-offs that shaped the app
/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.dec1.h3: Native iOS first rather than cross-platform
/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.dec1.p1: The classic temptation on a side project: Flutter or React Native to ship on iOS + Android at once. But the padel crowd — often high-end equipped, a racket at €200 and up — expects refinement.
/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.dec1.p2: I scoped a native iOS V1, components integrated into the system: gestures, animations, system dark mode, transitions. Cost: half the potential market not addressed in V1. Benefit: perceived quality consistent with the enthusiast player's expectations, gesture fluidity, an early-adopter base ready to recommend.
/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.dec2.h3: Smartwatch integration as a core axis, not a deferred option
/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.dec2.p1: MVP reflex: live score on the phone, like every competitor. But on a padel court, pulling out the phone between rallies = unbearable friction.
/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.dec2.p2: I made smartwatch integration (iOS & Android wearables) a core axis of V1: real-time score on the wrist, performance tracking, sync with the app. Benefit: immediate differentiation vs competitors who stay app-only, an experience aligned with the sporting gesture, higher perceived value.
/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.dec3.h3: A strong brand identity to stand out
/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.dec3.p1: With the market boom, several padel apps launch in parallel — the risk of blending into a mass of apple-green icons. I invested in brand identity as a strategic axis.
/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.dec3.p2: A «Tie Break» logo typeset with a tennis ball worked into the «I», a clay-court palette (deep orange-red) + ball yellow, immersive sports photography, a playful visual tone. Benefit: immediate recognition in the App Store, memorability from the first impression, brand equity reusable for product expansion.
/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.imp.li1: A native iOS padel app designed end to end: court directory, match page, live score, ranking among friends, smartwatch sync.
/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.imp.li2: A complete brand identity: logo, clay-court + ball-yellow palette, visual tone — a reusable base for product expansion.
/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.imp.li3: Smartwatch integration (iOS & Android wearables) framed as a core axis — immediate differentiation vs competitors.
/pages/work/tie-break.html.tb.imp.li4: A French padel market case study: a quantified opportunity (995 → 2,000 courts), three personas addressed, a documented growth mechanic.
